This is an illustrative application of the unit definition, not an additional experimental result. Merely stating that the sample contains 12 μmol of product would not say how quickly it formed.

The same logic applies when change is measured in concentration rather than amount: a concentration-per-time unit can describe velocity. State the conditions because different substrate concentrations or enzyme amounts can produce different rates. Also distinguish velocity from Km. Velocity belongs on the vertical rate axis, whereas Km is a substrate concentration read from the horizontal axis at one-half Vmax. Its units therefore cannot be substituted for rate units.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Objective W08-17 — Maximum velocity and units {#w08-lo17}

**Original objective:** What does maximum velocity refer to with respect to enzyme behaviour and what are the units of velocity (rate)

Explain Vmax, saturation, dependence on the amount of enzyme and the required units.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Vmax is the limiting maximum rate for the given amount of enzyme under specified conditions. At high substrate concentration, active sites are occupied most of the time and further substrate gives little additional rate increase. Vmax has rate units, such as μmol/min, not concentration units. It is not a universal number independent of how much active enzyme is present.

**Source:** Week 8 objectives, item 17; Lecture 8:23–8:26.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-lo17 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Vmax belongs to a specified enzyme amount and experimental situation. Once active sites are occupied most of the time, more substrate gives little extra rate; it is not evidence that all possible enzyme preparations have the same maximum. Because Vmax is a rate, its units must include time.

The rate curve initially rises because adding substrate gives the available enzyme more opportunities to act. At sufficiently high substrate concentration, active sites are occupied most of the time. The enzyme is then working near its limiting capacity, and additional substrate produces little further increase in rate. The plateau is the experimental indication of Vmax.

This maximum belongs to the enzyme amount and conditions being tested. It is not a universal maximum that remains identical when the amount of active enzyme changes. The word maximum also does not mean equilibrium: the enzyme can be turning over substrate rapidly near Vmax. Because the measured quantity is still a rate, report units such as μmol/min. A concentration unit alone would describe substrate availability, not the height of the velocity plateau.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Objective W08-18 — Km and units {#w08-lo18}

**Original objective:** What is the definition of Km and what are the units of Km

Define Km operationally and give its units. If Vmax is 60 μmol/min and v is 30 μmol/min at [S] = 3 mM, estimate Km.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Km is the substrate concentration at which v equals one-half Vmax for the Michaelis–Menten curve used here. Its units are concentration, such as mM. Half of 60 is 30 μmol/min, reached at 3 mM, so **Km = 3 mM**. Do not report Km in μmol/min or confuse it with the height of the plateau.

**Source:** Week 8 objectives, item 18; Lecture 8:25–8:26.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-lo18 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
First halve the maximum rate: 60/2 = 30 μmol/min. The supplied data place that rate at 3 mM substrate, so the concentration—not the rate—is Km. This sequence helps prevent copying the y-axis units into a value read from the x-axis.

Write the numerical steps with their units. The maximum rate is 60 μmol/min. One-half of that is **60/2 = 30 μmol/min**. The question states that this rate occurs at a substrate concentration of 3 mM, so the operational definition gives **Km = 3 mM**.

On a graph, you would move from 30 μmol/min on the vertical axis across to the curve, then down to the substrate axis. The final horizontal-axis reading is the answer. Reporting 30 μmol/min as Km confuses the rate used to locate the point with the concentration that defines Km. Reporting 60 μmol/min instead would give Vmax. This method uses the Michaelis–Menten relationship specified in the question and avoids making a stronger, unnecessary claim about binding affinity.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Objective W08-19 — NAD+/NADH {#w08-lo19}

**Original objective:** What is the role of NAD+ and NADH

Explain both forms of the carrier and why they must be recycled.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
NAD+ is the oxidized form and accepts reducing equivalents during substrate oxidation, becoming reduced NADH. NADH carries the electrons to later reactions and is oxidized back to NAD+. Regeneration of NAD+ permits further oxidation reactions. NADH is an electron carrier, not an enzyme, and is not interchangeable with ATP.

**Source:** Week 8 objectives, item 19; Lecture 8:28; Tutorial 5.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-lo19 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Think of NAD+ and NADH as consecutive states in a recycling loop. Substrate oxidation loads the carrier with electrons, and later electron donation restores the oxidized carrier. Without that restoration, the cell would lose the available NAD+ needed for further oxidation reactions.

Explain a complete carrier cycle rather than defining only the reduced form. NAD+ accepts reducing equivalents while a substrate is oxidized; the carrier becomes NADH. NADH can then donate those electrons in a later reaction and be oxidized back to NAD+. Restoring NAD+ makes it available to accept electrons from another substrate.

The recycling step matters because the supply of oxidized carrier is not unlimited. If NADH were never reoxidized, reactions needing NAD+ would eventually lack their electron acceptor even if fuel remained. This is why a carrier's role cannot be described simply as creating energy. It transfers electrons between processes. ATP serves a different activated-carrier role, and NADH is not a protein catalyst. Name the oxidized form, reduced form, and regeneration requirement to answer every part of the question.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

# Part C — Integrated Practice

### Integrated Question 1 — Thermodynamics and enzymes

A reaction has $\Delta G=-25$ kJ/mol but almost no product appears over one hour unless an enzyme is added. Does the enzyme make the reaction thermodynamically favorable? Explain.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The negative $\Delta G$ already means the reaction is thermodynamically favorable. The enzyme increases the rate by lowering activation energy; it does not make $\Delta G$ more negative or change the equilibrium constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-ix01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Use the observation to separate two questions. ΔG is already negative before the enzyme is added, so the enzyme cannot be credited with making the reaction favorable. The change in product formation instead shows that lowering the activation barrier can greatly increase reaction rate.

First interpret the number independently of the observation. A ΔG of −25 kJ/mol already makes the written direction exergonic under the stated conditions. The near absence of product after one hour therefore cannot be used to reclassify the reaction as endergonic. Instead, it suggests that conversion is slow on the timescale being observed.

Next ask what changes when enzyme is added. The enzyme supplies a lower-barrier route, so more substrate reaches the transition state and product forms more rapidly. The reactant and product free-energy levels are not changed by that catalytic effect. Thus the explanation must account for a change in speed while preserving the negative ΔG and the equilibrium constant. A clear answer ends by separating the two conclusions: the reaction was favorable before the enzyme was added, and the enzyme made the favorable reaction proceed faster, not more favorable.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 2 — Pathway reasoning

Reaction A converts X to Y with a positive $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$. Reaction B rapidly consumes Y to form Z and has a strongly negative $\Delta G$. Explain why X can still flow toward Z in a cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Because Y is continually removed, its concentration remains low, which can make the actual $\Delta G$ for X → Y favorable. In addition, the overall sequence X → Y → Z can have a negative total free-energy change. Metabolic pathway direction depends on the coupled sequence and actual concentrations, not on one isolated standard free-energy value.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-ix02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The pathway continually drains Y into Z, so X-to-Y is not operating with an isolated, accumulating product pool. Low Y can favor the actual forward reaction even when its standard value is positive. Assessing the whole sequence and the actual concentrations explains the continued flow toward Z.

The important distinction is that the question gives a **standard** value for X → Y but describes a functioning pathway in a cell. Reaction B continually removes Y, so the concentration conditions experienced by reaction A differ from those of an isolated standard-state reaction. Low Y can make the actual forward change favorable. The positive ΔG°′ therefore does not by itself prove that X cannot be converted to Y in this setting.

The second part of the reasoning concerns the whole sequence. Free-energy changes of properly combined steps are additive, so a sufficiently favorable downstream conversion can contribute to a favorable overall X → Z transformation. The question does not provide enough comparable numerical values to calculate an exact total, so the answer should remain qualitative. Do not say that reaction A's enzyme makes its standard value negative. Explain the shared intermediate, actual concentrations, and connected overall pathway instead.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 3 — Reading an enzyme curve

An enzyme reaches 50 μmol/min at very high substrate concentration. At 2 mM substrate, the rate is 25 μmol/min. Estimate Vmax and Km.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Vmax is approximately **50 μmol/min**. Half of Vmax is 25 μmol/min, which occurs at 2 mM substrate, so **Km ≈ 2 mM**.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-ix03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Identify the plateau before reading Km. The plateau gives Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min; half of it is 25 μmol/min, and the question places that rate at 2 mM substrate. Keeping each value attached to its own axis gives the correct units as well as the correct numbers.

Start with the high-substrate observation. A limiting rate near 50 μmol/min identifies **Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min**. Half of that rate is **50/2 = 25 μmol/min**. The second observation says that 25 μmol/min occurs at 2 mM substrate, so the substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity is **Km ≈ 2 mM**.

The distinction between the two answers is as important as the arithmetic. Vmax is a height on the rate axis and keeps the rate units μmol/min. Km is a position on the substrate-concentration axis and keeps the concentration units mM. It would be incorrect to report Km as 25 μmol/min, even though that number was needed to locate it. The approximations reflect that the stated high-substrate rate is being used as an estimate of the plateau. No additional information about equilibrium or the sign of ΔG can be inferred from these two kinetic readings.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 4 — Redox integration

A fuel molecule loses electrons to NAD+. Identify which molecule is oxidized, which is reduced, and what product is formed from NAD+.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The fuel molecule is **oxidized** because it loses electrons. NAD+ is **reduced** because it gains electrons, producing **NADH**.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-ix04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Follow the electrons from fuel to carrier. Their loss makes the fuel oxidized, and their acceptance makes NAD+ reduced. NADH is the product of that reduction; it is not a separate enzyme that causes the fuel to oxidize.

Assign the roles by following one transfer from beginning to end. The fuel starts with the electrons that are donated. Losing them is oxidation, so **the fuel is oxidized**. NAD+ receives the reducing equivalents. Gaining electrons is reduction, so **NAD+ is reduced**, and the resulting reduced carrier is **NADH**.

All three requested statements describe the same event from different perspectives; they are not three unrelated facts to memorize. The phrase fuel oxidation names the donor's change, while carrier reduction names the acceptor's change. Calling both partners oxidized would leave no electron recipient, and reversing the labels would contradict the direction given in the question. Notice also that the question does not require oxygen to be named for oxidation to occur. The electron-transfer definition is sufficient. Later donation by NADH can regenerate NAD+, but that recycling is a subsequent stage rather than the product-formation event asked about here.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 5 — Final synthesis

In four or five sentences, distinguish **free-energy change**, **activation energy**, **Vmax**, and **Km**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\Delta G$ describes the thermodynamic favorability and direction of a reaction under the specified conditions. Activation energy is the barrier that must be crossed to reach the transition state, and enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering this barrier. Vmax is the maximum reaction rate approached when enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate. Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax and therefore has concentration units.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w08-ix05 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Organize the four terms by the question each answers. ΔG concerns favorability, activation energy concerns the barrier, Vmax concerns the limiting rate, and Km identifies a substrate concentration on the rate curve. Separating these roles prevents using a kinetic measurement as an explanation of thermodynamic direction.

A useful way to construct the requested four- or five-sentence answer is to separate an energy diagram from a rate curve. On the energy diagram, **ΔG** compares product and reactant levels, whereas **activation energy** describes the barrier leading to the transition state. They address favorability and access to the reaction route, respectively. Lowering the barrier can increase speed without changing the endpoint difference.

On the rate curve, **Vmax** is the limiting velocity for the enzyme amount under the stated conditions. **Km** is the substrate concentration at half that velocity. Their units provide an immediate check: Vmax has rate units, such as μmol/min, while Km has concentration units, such as mM. Do not describe Km as half of Vmax; it is the concentration corresponding to half of Vmax. Keeping these two diagrams and their axes separate allows the final answer to define all four terms without treating a kinetic measurement as a thermodynamic quantity.

**Review:** [Week 8 study guide](../study-guides/week08-bioenergetics-enzymes.qmd).
:::
